one_liner: Hand-written WebAssembly text (WAT) image and utility algorithms; claims skeleton tracing beats an Emscripten build and vanilla JS.
what_it_does: A set of nine small programs written directly in WebAssembly text format and assembled with wabt's wat2wasm: Zhang-Suen thinning, Meijster distance transform, Suzuki-Abe contour finding, skeleton-to-polyline tracing, brownian trees, Wilson maze generation, a first-fit malloc, STL-like containers and random generators. Each .wat ships with a prebuilt .wasm that takes no imports. traceskeleton.wasm exposes a C-style API rather than the TraceSkeleton.fromCanvas interface of skeleton-tracing: setup(w,h), im_set(x,y,v) per pixel, thinning_zs(), trace_skeleton() returning a pointer to a linked list of polylines in linear memory, pl_*/pt_* accessors to walk it, and pls_destroy() to free it.
how_it_is_fast: The module carries no Emscripten runtime, WebIDL glue or string marshalling: the image lives as a byte array in linear memory and results stay as a linked list that JS walks through accessor exports. Tracing is the skeleton-tracing algorithm (recursive split of the image along the row or column of least resistance into 10-pixel chunks, a border walk of each chunk, then fragment merging) hand-translated to WAT with an inline implicit-free-list first-fit malloc. No benchmark isolates which of these choices produces the claimed gain.
when_to_use: A browser or Node page that needs binary-image skeleton tracing to polylines and wants a sub-kilobyte-class module (README: average binary about 900 bytes) instead of a SINGLE_FILE Emscripten bundle.
Small images where per-call overhead of the Emscripten build (string-encoded input, text-serialised polylines and rects parsed back with split/parseInt) would dominate.
Hosts with no build toolchain: the prebuilt .wasm files have no imports and can be instantiated directly.
Learning or teaching hand-written WAT: the sources are heavily commented and cite the papers they implement.
when_not_to_use: When you need a measured speedup: the only claim is one approximate README sentence with no harness, engine, hardware or input, and the repo times nothing but its own version.

Large images or skeletons with many points: every malloc scans the heap from address 0 (first-fit implicit free list) to place 12-byte point and 20-byte polyline nodes, so allocation cost grows with live nodes, unlike Emscripten's default allocator.
Native code: skeleton-tracing's C99 version (pthreads) is the reference implementation and its README puts it at 0.76 ms per run on a 300x149 image.
Concurrent use or several images per instance: all state (W, H, image pointer, heap) is module-global.
Projects that need maintenance or tests: 9 commits, last on 2020-08-26, only demo pages under tests/.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime; wabt wat2wasm to reassemble (compile.py calls ./wat2wasm)
integration.min_toolchain: any WebAssembly 1.0 engine (traceskeleton exports mutable globals MAX_ITER and CHUNK_SIZE); wabt to rebuild
integration.platforms: any WebAssembly host (browsers, Node.js); wasm32 linear memory starting at one 64 KiB page and grown on demand
integration.thread_safety: not documented; module-global state and a single heap make one instance usable by one caller at a time

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the 300% claim: skeleton-tracing's Emscripten build exposes only trace(DOMString img, w, h), which in one call runs Zhang-Suen thinning, tracing with SAVE_RECTS=1, std::to_string serialisation of polylines and rects, while its fromImageData/fromCanvas wrappers build the input string pixel by pixel and parse the output with split/parseInt; the only WAT timing in this repo (tests/traceskeleton.html) runs thinning_zs() and the im_set fill before starting a single Date() timer around trace_skeleton() and reads results after stopping it. A comparison through the public Emscripten API therefore timed thinning and marshalling on one side only; the method was never published. The vanilla JS library does expose traceSkeleton separately, but skeleton-tracing's own table puts vanilla JS (Node v12.10) at 38% of native C -O3, so a 5-6x win over it would make the WAT about twice as fast as native C, which points to non-comparable runs (one cold run, 1 ms Date() resolution, different input: horse.png is 400x328).

Licence mismatch: the repo LICENSE is the Unlicense and most .wat headers say Public Domain, but traceskeleton.wat is headed 'MIT License' and ends with the full MIT text (it ports MIT-licensed skeleton-tracing), so keep that notice when copying it.

setup() mallocs a new W*H image on every call without freeing the old one and does not zero it, so every pixel must be written with im_set; extend() drops the memory.grow result, so a failed grow traps on an out-of-bounds store instead of returning NULL.

thinning_zs stops as soon as either Zhang-Suen sub-iteration changes nothing (diff &= ...), not when a full pass changes nothing; the quirk is inherited from skeleton-tracing's C, C++ and JS versions, so output matches upstream but thinning can end early.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No sibling in hand-written-asm-kernels targets WebAssembly: FastMemcpy, FP-ASM, cespare/xxhash and the rest are native x86, Arm or Go assembly with published harnesses. Pick wasm-fun only when the code must run in a WebAssembly host and binary size matters; for native targets those siblings carry far better evidence.
verified_claims_summary: The README says traceskeleton.wat is '~300% faster than the version complied with emscripten (and ~10x smaller), ~500% faster than vanilla Javascript', with no engine, hardware, Emscripten version, input or harness; the comparator is skeleton-tracing's -O3, closure-compiled, WebIDL-glued Emscripten build and its vanilla JS port. Nothing was re-measured, and the repo's only timing code covers the WAT version alone and excludes thinning and I/O that the Emscripten path includes.
status_note: Abandoned since 2020-08-26 (9 commits, no issues filed); the small, dependency-free sources are easy to vendor under the Unlicense, except traceskeleton.wat, which carries an MIT notice.
